read.sections.0.text.source: The Banda Islands are small islands in eastern Indonesia. For hundreds of years, they were the only place in the world where nutmeg trees grew. The tree's seed gives nutmeg, and the red skin around the seed gives a spice called mace. Buyers far away paid a lot for both. Traders came from Indonesia, China, India, Persia and Arabia. Later, ships came from Portugal, the Netherlands and England. Bandanese leaders were skilled traders, and they chose whom to sell to. Selling spice also paid for food, because the islands grew very little.
read.sections.0.text.back: The Banda Islands are small islands in eastern Indonesia. For hundreds of years, the islands were the only place in the world that had nutmeg trees. The tree's seed produces nutmeg, and the red skin around the seed produces a spice called mace. Buyers in faraway places paid a lot for both. Traders came from Indonesia, China, India, Persia and Arabia. Later, ships came from Portugal, the Netherlands and England. Banda's leaders were skilled traders, and they chose whom they sold to. Money from selling spice was also used to buy food, because the islands produced very little food.
read.sections.0.text.note: "Bandanese" is "orang Banda" throughout; the checker's name warning for "Bandanese" is expected.

read.sections.0.simpler.source: The Banda Islands are in Indonesia. For a long time, only Banda had nutmeg trees. Nutmeg is a spice from the seed. Mace is a spice from the red skin on the seed. People far away paid a lot for them. Traders came from many places in Asia, and later from Europe. Banda's leaders were good traders. They chose who to sell to.
read.sections.0.simpler.back: The Banda Islands are in Indonesia. For a long time, only Banda had nutmeg trees. Nutmeg is a spice from the seed. Mace is a spice from the red skin on the seed. People in faraway places paid a lot for them. Traders came from many places in Asia, and later from Europe. Banda's leaders were clever traders. They chose whom they sold to.

read.sections.1.text.source: The Dutch East India Company, called the VOC, wanted a monopoly. It wanted to be the only buyer of Banda's nutmeg, so no one else could compete. In 1609, a VOC fleet came to Banda Neira, one of the islands, and began to build a fort. The people there refused the company's demands, and years of fighting followed. In 1621, a VOC force led by Jan Pieterszoon Coen attacked the islands. Many Bandanese people were killed. Others were enslaved or forced to leave. Some escaped to other islands, where people kept Banda's history alive in songs and dances. After 1621, the VOC gave the land to settlers, and enslaved people were forced to grow the nutmeg.
read.sections.1.text.back: The Dutch East India Company, called the VOC, wanted a monopoly. The VOC wanted to be the only buyer of Banda's nutmeg, so that nobody else could compete. In 1609, a VOC fleet came to Banda Neira, one of the islands, and started to build a fort. The people there refused the company's demands, and fighting went on for years. In 1621, a VOC force led by Jan Pieterszoon Coen attacked the islands. Many Banda people were killed. Others were enslaved or forced to leave. Some escaped to other islands, and there people kept Banda's history alive through songs and dances. After 1621, the VOC gave the land to settlers, and enslaved people were forced to grow the nutmeg.
read.sections.1.text.note: "Enslaved" is "diperhambakan" (standard) and "dijadikan hamba" (simpler); "settlers" is "peneroka", which in Malaysia can also suggest FELDA settlers: "pendatang" or "penempatan peneroka" are alternatives.

read.sections.1.simpler.source: A Dutch company called the VOC came to Banda. It wanted a monopoly. It wanted to be the only buyer of nutmeg. In 1609, it began to build a fort. The people of Banda said no. They fought for years. In 1621, the VOC attacked again. Many Bandanese people were killed. Others were made slaves or forced to leave. Some escaped to other islands. They kept Banda's history alive in songs and dances. Then enslaved people had to grow the nutmeg.
read.sections.1.simpler.back: A Dutch company called the VOC came to Banda. The VOC wanted a monopoly. The VOC wanted to be the only buyer of nutmeg. In 1609, the VOC started to build a fort. The people of Banda said no. They fought for years. In 1621, the VOC attacked again. Many Banda people were killed. Others were made slaves or forced to leave. Some escaped to other islands. They kept Banda's history alive through songs and dances. Later, slaves were forced to grow the nutmeg.

read.sections.2.text.source: The second picture is a painting of Banda Neira from about 1662, more than 40 years after the attack. The VOC paid a painters' workshop in the Netherlands to make it. It shows forts, a ship, houses and neat rows of nutmeg trees. It does not show the people who were harmed, or the people who worked in those gardens. The painting shows the company's perspective. Coen's own reports from 1621 are company sources too. In his letters, he wrote that almost nobody escaped, but that was not true. So historians compare sources, and they also listen to the songs and stories that Bandanese people passed down.
read.sections.2.text.back: The second picture is a painting of Banda Neira from about 1662, more than 40 years after the attack. The VOC paid a painters' workshop in the Netherlands to make it. The painting shows forts, a ship, houses and neat rows of nutmeg trees. The painting does not show the people who were harmed, or the people who worked in those gardens. The painting shows the company's perspective. Coen's own reports from 1621 are also company sources. In his letters, he wrote that almost nobody escaped, but that was not true. So historians compare sources, and they also listen to the songs and stories passed down by Banda people.

sensitiveNotes.0.source: This lesson covers the VOC's conquest of Banda in 1621: mass killing, enslavement and forced removal. The Dutch National Archives' teaching page is titled “Genocide op Banda (1621)”. Learner text states it plainly, once, with no detail and no death toll; sources give different numbers (the archives: up to 15,000 people before, about 1,000 left on the islands; the Rijksmuseum: all 15,000 killed or driven away), so never ask learners to learn a figure. Some learners may have lived through violence or forced displacement: say before part 2 what it covers, let anyone read the simpler text or step away, and never ask learners about their own or their family's experiences of war, displacement, their country, religion or ethnicity. Don't present the events as a disagreement with two equal sides, and never invent a Bandanese first-person quotation. The TED-Ed video describes the violence in far more detail than the lesson (see its note): preview it first.
sensitiveNotes.0.back: This lesson covers the VOC's conquest of Banda in 1621: mass killing, enslavement and forced removal. The Dutch National Archives' teaching page is titled “Genocide op Banda (1621)” (Genocide on Banda). Learner text states it plainly, once only, with no detail and no death toll; sources give different numbers (the archives: up to 15,000 people before, about 1,000 remaining on the islands; the Rijksmuseum: all 15,000 killed or driven out), so never ask learners to memorise a number. Some learners may have experienced violence or been forced to move: say before part 2 what it covers, let anyone read the simpler text or step away for a while, and never ask learners about their own or their family's experiences of war, displacement, their country, religion or ethnicity. Don't present these events as a disagreement between two equal sides, and never make up a quotation of a Banda person's words. The TED-Ed video describes the violence in far more detail than this lesson (see its note): watch it first.
sensitiveNotes.0.note: Sensitive lesson (mass killing, enslavement, forced removal): a Malaysian reviewer should read the learner text and this note first. "Genosid di Banda" glosses the Dutch title; "genosid" is the DBP word for genocide.

educatorNotes.0.source: Aim: learners name the VOC's monopoly and the harm it brought, and say whose account a company source leaves out. Evidence move (brief 3B): read Coen's report as a company source (he led the attack, and the archives show his claim that almost nobody escaped was false: about 1,700 Bandanese escaped), then look at the later commissioned painting. A sound answer names the monopoly and the harm and identifies a missing account. Misconception to catch: a fort or an orderly ship in the painting does not prove trade was voluntary or that the VOC caused no harm. Banda's history did not end in 1621: people who escaped kept it alive, for example in the Kei Islands, through songs and dances such as the Wanar dance (Dutch National Archives).
educatorNotes.0.back: Aim: learners name the VOC's monopoly and the harm it brought, and say whose account a company source does not include. Evidence step (brief 3B): read Coen's report as a company source (he led the attack, and the archives show that his claim that almost nobody escaped was false: about 1,700 Banda people escaped), then look at the painting ordered later. A good answer names the monopoly and its harm and identifies an account that is missing. Misconception to catch: an orderly fort or ship in the painting does not prove that the trade was voluntary or that the VOC caused no harm. Banda's history did not end in 1621: people who escaped kept it alive, for example in the Kei Islands, through songs and dances such as the Wanar dance (Dutch National Archives).

educatorNotes.1.source: Source caveats: the Dutch National Archives says its collection holds no sources with Bandanese voices, so every archive source on Banda tells the story from a colonial view. Its page shows Coen's 6 May 1621 report on the decision to starve out Banda Besar; the lesson describes it only in general terms and never quotes it. The Rijksmuseum says the painting was commissioned by the VOC's Amsterdam chamber from the Vingboons workshop before 30 April 1663, probably for the directors' meeting room, and was based on company maps: Neira never had five nutmeg gardens, and the hills behind are imagined. Before the VOC, the Westfries Museum says Dutch traders at first paid port fees and bought spice like other visitors, which helps show the change from trade to force.
educatorNotes.1.back: Source caveats: the Dutch National Archives says its collection contains no sources with the voices of Banda people, so every archive source about Banda tells the story from the colonisers' point of view. Its page shows Coen's report dated 6 May 1621 about the decision to starve Banda Besar into surrender; this lesson describes it only in general terms and never quotes it. The Rijksmuseum says that the painting was ordered by the VOC's Amsterdam branch from the Vingboons workshop before 30 April 1663, probably for the directors' meeting room, and was based on company maps: Neira never had five nutmeg gardens, and the hills at the back were only imagined. Before the VOC, the Westfries Museum says that Dutch traders at first paid port taxes and bought spices like other visitors, and this helps show the change from trade to force.
educatorNotes.1.note: "The decision to starve out Banda Besar" is "keputusan untuk melaparkan Banda Besar sehingga menyerah"; check the verb "melaparkan".
